newsitem.title: BOSNIA: Reports of coercion in Bosnia voter registration.
newsitem.headline: Reports of coercion in Bosnia voter registration.

text.p: Some Bosnian voters are coming under pressure from authorities to register for local elections as political parties try to stack the odds in their favour, workers and international monitors said on Tuesday.
The main Moslem, Serb and Croat nationalist parties are keen to obtain a high number of registered voters to assert control over territory contested during the 1992-95 war.

Employees at a hospital in the central, Moslem-dominated town of Zenica said they were coerced into signing up to vote by the hospital director who required them to show proof that they had registered, a local television station reported.
The hospital director told nurses of each department to order employees to register and then make lists of voters, independent Zetelt television reported.
Zetelt obtained one of the orders issued last month by a chief nurse of the orthopedic and traumatology clinic.

"This is violating my voter rights on two accounts -- the right to register or not and the right to choose which municipality (to vote in)," a hospital worker, who asked not to be named, told Reuters.
The employee said he was a refugee from Serb-controlled territory who was now living in predominantly Moslem Zenica in Bosnia's Moslem-Croat federation.
He said he chose not to vote in his pre-war municipality because the party he supports is not on the ballot.
"When I showed my registration slip, they asked me why did I not register in my pre-war municipality. That's intimidation," he said.
The hospital director was unavailable for comment.

Municipal elections, considered vital for Bosnia's peacetime reconciliation, were postponed last year because of registration abuses orchestrated by Bosnian Serb authorities, who are anxious to seal wartime territorial gains.
A spokesman for the Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe (OSCE), which is overseeing Bosnia's local vote, confirmed it had received complaints from Zenica.
"No form of coercion of any kind is acceptable and there is a fine line between encouraging people to register and using some sort of intimidation to register," spokesman David Foley said.

The complaints prompted the OSCE to warn Zenica authorities last week about possible coercion. An earlier OSCE letter to Zenica authorities, discussing low registration turnout, might have created a misunderstanding, Foley said.
"I think it was a question of bit of over-zealousness by municipal authorities in requiring people to show their documentation, their registration receipts," he said.

An OSCE commission penalised the ruling party in Bosnian Serb-controlled territory last month after authorities were found trying to falsify registration documents and harassing international supervisors.
